claude_take: There's a quiet theme of control today: the FTC compelling OpenAI and Anthropic to open their books on security incidents, Mexico ordering platforms to police content for minors, and Richemont trying to lock down its own diamond supply by joining a bid for De Beers. But control is selective about where it shows up. Netflix cut a thousand jobs while insisting its business has never been stronger, and French filmmakers are warning that budget cuts could simply erase 400 films nobody will notice are missing until they're gone. The common thread is institutions reaching for more oversight precisely where it's easiest to assert, and quietly withdrawing it where it would actually cost something.
claude_take_title: 400 Films Nobody Will Notice Are Missing

items.headline: FTC Sends Formal Subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic Over Security Incidents
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission issued civil investigative demands, each running more than 50 pages, to OpenAI and Anthropic this week, seeking documents on security incidents, safeguards, marketing materials and privacy policies. The move escalates the FTC's AI-safety probe disclosed in late September into a formal compulsory process, with the agency also planning to push senior executives to testify and to send further demands to other labs. OpenAI said it would engage constructively with the agency; Anthropic has not commented.

items.headline: Google Expands Its Paid AI-News Licensing Program to More Than 400 Publishers
items.summary: Google said its program paying news organizations for content used in generative AI features has grown from a small 2025 pilot to more than 400 publishers worldwide, with CNN, Axios and the Financial Times among the latest to join. Google said the resulting AI features will carry clear attribution and direct links back to source articles. The expansion marks one of the AI industry's largest coordinated efforts yet to formalize payment to the publishers whose journalism trains and feeds AI products.

items.headline: Netflix Cuts About 1,000 Jobs in Its Largest Layoff Round Since 2022
items.summary: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told staff in a Wednesday memo that the company is cutting roughly 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 positions, hitting product, technology, legal and HR teams hardest. The executives framed the cuts as a matter of focus rather than weakness, insisting the business remains strong and on track to hit its full-year forecast, even as the company's third-quarter outlook had come in below Wall Street's expectations.

items.headline: 170 French Filmmakers, Including Jacques Audiard and Justine Triet, Warn 2027 Budget Could Wipe Out 400 Films
items.summary: Around 170 directors, including Jacques Audiard, Justine Triet, Costa-Gavras and Michel Hazanavicius, signed a public letter warning that France's draft 2027 budget could cut roughly 750 million euros from film financing between 2028 and 2032, threatening the production of some 400 films. The signatories singled out a proposed doubling of VAT on Canal+ subscriptions and a cut to France Télévisions' funding, both still under debate in the National Assembly, as the measures most likely to hollow out the country's public-private film financing system.

items.headline: Mexico Orders Social Platforms to Shield Minors From Violent and Sexual Content
items.summary: President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree requiring digital platforms, including Meta, TikTok, X and Google, to detect and remove content involving hate speech, extremism, sexual violence, suicide and self-harm before it reaches minors, rather than only responding to complaints. The decree, which followed a deadly attack by two former students at a school in Coahuila, gives platforms a month to comply; officials said it is mandatory but not itself punitive, while warning they would back legislation to penalize noncompliance. Meta said it would review the decree; TikTok and X had not yet responded publicly.

items.headline: Pennsylvania Reports a Sixth Measles-Related Death as US Cases Pass 4,000
items.summary: A Franklin County coroner confirmed the sixth measles-associated death in Pennsylvania this year, a 39-year-old woman with underlying health conditions who died of a probable cardiac event linked to measles complications. The state has now confirmed over 1,200 cases and more than 200 hospitalizations in its outbreak, while the CDC says the national case count has topped 4,000, the highest since 1991. Pennsylvania's health department said it is still reviewing the latest death to confirm it meets the state's criteria for a measles-associated fatality.

items.headline: Cartier Owner Richemont Weighs Joining a Consortium Bid for De Beers
items.summary: Richemont, the Swiss luxury group behind Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, is in talks to join a consortium bidding roughly $1 billion for De Beers, the diamond miner Anglo American is selling. Jewelry retailer Signet is also reported to be weighing a stake in the same group. A successful deal would hand Richemont direct influence over a key upstream link in its own jewelry supply chain, though any agreement still depends on Botswana's government, which holds a right of first refusal over the miner's sale.

items.headline: Preprint Study Finds ADHD's Link to Higher Mortality Is Largely Explained by Anxiety and Depression
items.summary: A new analysis of more than 52,000 US adults followed for a median of nearly eight years found that ADHD was associated with a markedly higher risk of death, but that co-occurring anxiety and depression accounted for the majority of that elevated risk, with socioeconomic and lifestyle factors explaining comparatively little. The study is a preprint and has not yet been peer-reviewed, but it points toward mental-health comorbidities, rather than ADHD itself, as the more actionable target for reducing excess mortality in adults with the condition.

items.headline: Levinas's Face of the Other
items.headline_fr: Le visage de l'Autre chez Levinas
items.summary: Emmanuel Levinas argued that ethics does not begin with abstract principles or self-interested reasoning, but with the direct, pre-rational encounter with another person's face, which issues an infinite, unchosen demand: do not kill me. For Levinas, this encounter precedes and grounds every later rule about right and wrong, reversing a Western tradition that typically locates morality in autonomous reason. The idea still matters because it locates moral responsibility in vulnerability itself rather than in calculation, and it implicitly challenges any system, screen, or mediated exchange that lets people interact without ever truly facing one another.
items.summary_fr: Pour Emmanuel Levinas, l'éthique ne commence pas par des principes abstraits ou par un calcul d'intérêt, mais par la rencontre directe et préréflexive du visage d'autrui, qui m'impose une exigence infinie et non choisie : ne me tue pas. Cette rencontre précède et fonde toute règle ultérieure sur le bien et le mal, à l'inverse d'une tradition occidentale qui ancre généralement la morale dans la raison autonome. L'idée reste précieuse aujourd'hui, car elle situe la responsabilité morale dans la vulnérabilité elle-même plutôt que dans le calcul, et interroge en creux tout système ou tout échange médiatisé qui permet aux gens de se côtoyer sans jamais vraiment se faire face.
